title: Secular Carmelites
hookLine: Carmel's prayer, carried home by people with jobs, kids and bills

cards: Early morning, a kitchen table. Lunch boxes half packed, a phone face down, a mug going cold. A woman sits with a small book open, eyes closed, while the kettle ticks.
In an hour she'll be at work; tonight there's a parents' meeting. She isn't a nun, and she'll never live behind a grille.
But she has made a promise to live by the spirit of Carmel, and this quiet stretch before the day starts is part of that promise. Today, the Carmelites who live at home.

teach.b: First, who they are. Carmel has friars and nuns, and it also has laypeople, married or single, with ordinary jobs and families, who belong to the order as Secular Carmelites. Secular here doesn't mean unreligious.
It means living in the everyday world rather than in a monastery. Second, the promise.

After a time of formation, a Secular Carmelite makes a promise before the community to follow the gospel in the spirit of Carmel: its love of prayer, its devotion to Mary, its friendship with saints like Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross.
They meet in local communities for prayer and study, then go home to their lives. Third, the center: mental prayer.

Their rule of life asks for a regular time each day of silent prayer, the friendly conversation with God that Teresa described, along with parts of the Church's daily prayer, the Liturgy of the Hours.
It isn't extra busyness. It's a still point in a full life. Fourth, why it matters.
Luke's Gospel tells of two sisters, Martha busy serving, and Mary listening.
In the Douay-Rheims: "And she had a sister called Mary, who sitting also at the Lord's feet, heard his word." Secular Carmelites don't have to choose one sister over the other.
They live in Martha's house, the dishes and the deadlines, with a Mary-shaped space inside it. The desert of Carmel, it turns out, can fit into a kitchen.

how: Secular Carmelites meet in local communities for prayer, study and formation, make a promise to live the Carmelite spirit, and keep a daily time of silent prayer along with parts of the Liturgy of the Hours.

o: laypeople who live Carmel's prayer at home and work
friars who serve outside the monastery as pastors
nuns who leave the cloister to teach in schools

s: it means living in the world rather than in a monastery.
Secular Carmelites can be married and have jobs
they are laypeople who belong to the order and live at home.
they only pray when they meet as a group
their rule of life asks for silent prayer each day, at home.

games.q: you're a parent with a job and a full house, and Carmel's prayer draws you. what does the Secular Order offer?
o: leave your family for a convent.
give up: Carmel is only for nuns and friars.
make a promise and live Carmel's prayer at home.
games.why: Secular Carmelites belong to Carmel by a promise and keep its prayer in ordinary homes, Martha's house with Mary's quiet inside.

practice: Find one place in your home that could be your prayer corner, a chair, a step, a spot by a window, and in your mind sit there now, letting the house stay busy around you; nothing needs to stop for you to be still.
If you pray, speak to God simply, as to a friend; if you don't, just rest in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Secular Carmelites. Laypeople who belong to the Carmelite family by a promise, and live its prayer in ordinary homes and jobs. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: carmel at home. A corner like that can hold a daily stretch of quiet, even twenty minutes, while the house stays loud. See you tomorrow.
